items.body:
Stéphane is genuinely invested in his work within the company; he is technically very good at what he does (full-stack on Microsoft technologies), with solid skills across backend development (.NET), frontend (Angular) and DevOps (Azure and its whole ecosystem).

On a human level, he is someone you quickly come to appreciate and want to work with. He handles pressure well and shows great autonomy on his projects.

I recommend him without hesitation!

Stéphane is a developer with high technical skills around Microsoft development technologies, in .NET as well as Angular. Code quality and optimization are fundamentals of his work. He is genuinely full-stack. He drives proposals on both front and back to find agile, durable solutions, and he is good at analyzing malfunctions and joining projects already under way.

Beyond his technical skills, he is curious and has a real aptitude for teamwork: he will support and grow other developers without doing the work in their place. Stéphane has a good command of the Scrum agile methodology.

Stéphane is a highly competent tech lead. He masters the front end, the back end, databases, CI/CD and the cloud alike. He puts the architecture and design patterns in place and optimizes constantly. He talks to technical and functional people equally well. In short, a gem :-)

projectScenes.name: OPEN SPACE.EXE — software-rendered FPS engine
projectScenes.role: Author — from scratch, driving an AI
projectScenes.description: A DOOM-style (BSP) engine with no WebGL: two render backends (8-thread CPU via SharedArrayBuffer, WebGPU), voxel sprites, hand-authored levels.
projectScenes.problem: A DOOM-style engine in the browser, without WebGL, means rasterising everything yourself: projecting the geometry, mapping textures, depth-sorting, all in real time on a JavaScript CPU. Written naively, that pipeline can't keep up.
projectScenes.approach: A real BSP pipeline: binary space partition, depth sorting with no z-buffer. Two interchangeable backends render the same world pixel-for-pixel, a measured parity: a CPU rasteriser spread over 8 threads via SharedArrayBuffer, and a WebGPU/WGSL backend. Voxel sprites, hand-made levels built through a RoomBuilder authoring layer.
highlights: Software BSP engine written from scratch, no WebGL
Two backends: 8-thread CPU (SharedArrayBuffer) and WebGPU/WGSL
CPU ↔ WebGPU pixel parity, measured
Voxel sprites, hand-made levels
RoomBuilder authoring layer: rooms, connections, automatic winding
projectScenes.imageAlt: Top-down map of an OPEN SPACE.EXE level, with rooms, portals and enemies

projectScenes.name: NgSharp v3 — a template engine for .NET
projectScenes.description: Angular-style interpreted templates, format-agnostic: parses any text file with deep HTML awareness. Zero dependencies, Native AOT compatible.
projectScenes.problem: Rendering HTML server-side in .NET usually means code generation: Razor compiles its views through Roslyn. That compilation weighs on cold start and rules out Native AOT.
projectScenes.approach: NgSharp interprets instead of compiling. It parses the template into an AST on first use, caches the tree, then renders by walking it: no Roslyn, no IL emit, so cold start is instant and the reflection-free path stays Native AOT compatible. One dependency: System.Text.Json.
highlights: Angular-style syntax: interpolation, pipes, @if/@for, safe navigation
Interpreted: AST cached, no generated code
Native AOT and trimming compatible, reflection-free
Immutable, thread-safe AST: parsed once, rendered concurrently
Purpose-built HTML parser, a single runtime dependency (System.Text.Json)

projectScenes.name: FluentGraphQL — a query builder for .NET
projectScenes.description: Fluent, type-safe GraphQL queries on the .NET side, no generated schema. Performance tracked by reproducible benchmarks committed in the repo.
projectScenes.problem: Generated GraphQL clients freeze the query at compile time. The moment you compose one at runtime (optional fields, filters coming from user input), you fall back to string assembly, untyped and unverifiable.
projectScenes.approach: The API chains, reading field names via CallerArgumentExpression with no per-field expression tree. LINQ filters become type-safe where clauses by parsing a single expression tree per query, never compiled. One runtime dependency: System.Text.Json.
highlights: Fluent API for queries and mutations
Type-safe LINQ filters translated to GraphQL clauses
A single runtime dependency (System.Text.Json)
Expression tree parsed once per query, never compiled
Reproducible benchmarks committed in the repo

projectScenes.name: Universe Map — a 3D map of the Universe
projectScenes.description: Continuous zoom across five orders of magnitude, 10,000 stars in a single draw call, local ephemerides and an eclipse engine checked against NASA data.
projectScenes.problem: Rendering the Universe at true scale breaks 3D engines. From the metre to the light-year, distances no longer fit in a single floating-point frame, and drawing thousands of stars collapses the framerate.
projectScenes.approach: A continuous semantic zoom across five orders of magnitude, with a reversible parent frame so scales are never mixed in one coordinate space. Nearby stars fit into a single draw call through instancing. Ephemerides and the eclipse engine run locally, with no backend, checked against NASA data.
highlights: Continuous zoom from the Solar System to the Cosmicflows-4 cosmic web
10,000 stars in a single draw call (instancing)
Ephemerides and eclipses computed in the browser, no backend
Aug 12, 2026 eclipse verified against NASA data
Data labelled: measured, calculated, simulated, illustrative

paragraphs: My name is Stéphane De Todaro. Technical lead and full-stack architect with 9 years of experience — a role that grew gradually: first because someone had to ship what we built, then out of genuine pleasure for industrializing.
Day-to-day: C# / .NET for APIs and services, TypeScript / Angular for interfaces, Terraform on Azure. And regularly, Dart / Flutter when a mobile project shows up.

I believe in frequent releases, tests that actually cover, pipelines that don't lie, and the fact that "it works on my machine" is not a proof. My colleagues describe me as someone who ships and who teaches.
